analysis.one_liner: Lets states and cities regulate towing companies that take cars without the owner's consent.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a vote, hearing, or any cosponsors during the 109th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently lets states and cities regulate only the prices that tow companies charge when they take a car without the owner's consent. This bill would broaden that permission, letting states and local governments write their own rules for those towing operations altogether — for example, requiring proper signage, documentation, or consent procedures. The bill never advanced past its referral to a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners and drivers, especially in cities where private tow companies haul away vehicles without the owner's consent and charge steep fees to get them back. Consumers would gain if state or local governments choose to write anti-predatory-towing rules that federal preemption currently blocks.

how_it_helps.text: Under current federal law, states and local governments may regulate only the price of towing done without the vehicle owner's consent; this bill strikes those limits so they can regulate the towing operations themselves [S2][S3].

That would let cities and states address practices the bill's title calls predatory — such as towing cars from lots without adequate notice or authorization — with rules on conduct, not just rates [S1][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Towing companies that profit from removing vehicles without the owner's consent would bear the cost of complying with whatever state and local rules governments choose to adopt. The bill itself imposes no rules; it only removes a federal barrier to them.

drawbacks.text: Deregulation advocates argue federal uniformity prevents a patchwork of 50 different state towing regimes for interstate motor carriers, which is why federal law preempts most state regulation of for-hire transportation [S3].
The bill is a permission slip, not a protection: it does nothing on its own, and its value depends entirely on individual states and cities choosing to act [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but modest: it removes a federal preemption barrier so local governments can police towing abuses, which mostly hit drivers with modest incomes through surprise fees and lost time. The cost falls on towing firms that profit from nonconsensual tows, and the main downside is potential regulatory patchwork. The bill's weakness is design, not substance — it does nothing by itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to its highways subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Moran introduced the bill on March 8, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day [S1][S5].
The next day it was sent to the Subcommittee on Highways, Transit and Pipelines, which took no further action on it [S5].
No cosponsor signed on, no committee vote was ever recorded, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Towing companies that benefit from the existing federal limit on state and local regulation are better off, since the barrier remains. State and local governments and drivers gained nothing, because no state ever received the added authority.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to show a partisan split, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so support never materialized at all.

industries.note: These firms profit from taking cars without the owner's consent and charging recovery fees. The bill would expose their operations to state and local regulation beyond price caps, and its failure leaves the federal shield in place.
